s: Q U A N T I T A T I V E
India's only listed copper miner rides the copper supercycle
Hindustan Copper reported a record September quarter on 11 November: 1)
consolidated revenue from operations of Rs 1,175 crore, up 63.7% year on year
and 25.5% quarter on quarter, with consolidated net profit of Rs 518 crore
(+181.9% y/y; +47.0% q/q) and EBITDA of Rs 703 crore, a 59.8% margin; 2)
over the first half, revenue rose 71% to Rs 2,112 crore and consolidated net
profit rose 174% to Rs 871 crore (EPS of Rs 9.00); and 3) the shares reacted
hard and briefly — as much as 7% higher intraday on 12 November, closing
+2.2% on the day, then sliding steadily to Rs 425.85 by 19-Nov-26 (-44% from
The quarter was copper: the LME cash price hit a record $14,797 a tonne in
September and averaged about $14,532 a tonne in October before retreating to
$13,992 a tonne by 10 November, and HCL captured it with record volumes —
3.67 million tonnes of ore (+6%) and 27,421 tonnes of metal in concentrate in
FY26 (+9%, the best in seven years). The balance sheet is now geared to
delivery: an approved Rs 7,189 crore capex programme for FY26-FY30 (to 12.2
million tonnes of ore by FY30), funded partly by a proposed QIP of up to 9.70
crore shares (~10%) after the government sold 6.00% in August, taking the
promoter holding to 60.14%. Our Dec-27 PT is Rs 145 on a three-stage DCF
(WACC 13.7%, terminal margin 30%) rolled forward less assumed Rs 3.36 of
dividends; the reverse DCF says today's price needs an 8.15% WACC — an
8.15% discount rate does not describe a single-product Indian miner. We initiate
Underweight. The call would be wrong if copper holds above $14,000 a tonne
into FY28 and the 12.2 MTPA ramp lands on time and on budget.

Q U A N T I T A T I V E
Hindustan Copper is India’s only integrated copper miner: ore at Malanjkhand and other
mines, concentrators, smelters and refineries, down to continuous copper wire rods.
Copper is in a structural deficit — mine supply has lagged demand for electrification,
power grids, renewables and EVs, and grades everywhere are falling — and HCL is the
only listed way to own that torque in India. That is the bull case, and it is real. The
problem is the price: at Rs 425.85 the shares trade at 22.5x our FY27E EPS of Rs 18.88,
9.4x book and 15.1x FY27E EV/EBITDA, after a 6.00% government OFS in August
and with a proposed QIP of up to 9.70 crore shares still to land. Through-cycle
fundamentals do not meet that number. We initiate Underweight.
The quarter was copper, captured with discipline
Consolidated revenue rose 63.7% to Rs 1,175 crore and net profit 181.9% to Rs 518
crore. EBITDA margin hit 59.8%, from 39.3% in Q2 FY26, as record LME prices met
the first full year of the cost program. Receivables rose 114% y/y to Rs 286 crore —
customers stretching terms at record prices — and inventories built 14%, so cash
conversion (CFO/PAT, 97%) was fine but not free; FY27 capex of Rs 1,422 crore is
well ahead of H1’s Rs 295 crore.
The plan is real, huge and not self-funded
HCL’s April 2026 Annual Plan targets 4.71 Mt of ore this year, 5.18 Mt in FY28, 5.90
Mt in FY29 and 12.20 Mt by FY30 — near-tripling Malanjkhand and new mines. Capex
of Rs 6,738 crore is planned for FY27-FY30 (Rs 7,189 crore including FY26). FY28
free cash flow turns negative even in our base case (capex Rs 1,994 crore vs CFO of
roughly Rs 1,990 crore). The tab is expected to be funded by the QIP (up to 9.70 crore
shares, ~10%) and Rs 500 crore of approved NCDs. Delivery is everything: contractors,
approvals, and a CPSE board that has had no Independent Directors since November
2024 and no Woman Director since March 2025, per the auditors’ Other Matters
HCL is a Ministry of Mines enterprise and 60.14% government-owned after the August
OFS. It produces at world-class ore grades but at sub-scale, and its cost structure reflects
PSU norms. FY26 dividend was Rs 2.86 (interim Rs 1.00 paid 5-Mar-26; final Rs 1.86
recommended May-26). The Vision 2030 plan projects PAT of Rs 600 crore (FY27), Rs
669 crore (FY28), Rs 663 crore (FY29) and Rs 1,568 crore (FY30) and dividends of Rs
177-470 crore — all set before the copper spike; our numbers are higher near-term
(copper) and rely on the same volume ramp.
Our Dec-27 PT of Rs 145 comes from a three-stage DCF (H2 FY27E + FY28E +
FY29E, then FY30E-FY34E, then a fade to a 30% terminal EBIT margin at 5.0%
growth) at a 13.7% WACC, rolled forward less assumed Rs 3.36 of dividends to Dec-27
(FY26 final Rs 1.86 + assumed Rs 1.50 FY27 interim). On the 5-year monthly beta (cost
of equity 15.6%) the value is Rs 120. Reverse DCF: the price implies an 8.15% WACC
— a number appropriate to government securities, not to a single-commodity miner.

Risks to Rating and Price Target
Copper price and margins: our base case fades copper to $12,000/t (FY28) and $11,000/t
(FY29) with EBIT margins of 52%/51% of total income, from 54.0% in H1 FY27. If
copper holds above $14,000 into FY28, FY28E EPS is Rs 21+ and the stock’s multiples
print looser than our PT implies. The PT risk and the thesis risk are the same variable.
Governance and control: the board has had no Independent Directors since 3-Nov-2024 and
no Woman Director since 22-Mar-2025, so the Audit Committee is not validly constituted
and results are approved by the Board alone (auditor’s Other Matters). This discount is
The expansion must be paid for and built: Rs 6,738 crore of capex over FY27-30 cannot be
funded by internal accruals at our numbers (FY28 FCF is negative). The funding route (QIP
of up to 9.70 crore shares, ~10% dilution, undated; Rs 500 crore approved NCDs) and
execution of the 12.2 MTPA ramp are both open questions.

Receivables and working capital: trade receivables rose 114% y/y to Rs 286 crore at 30-
Sep-26, and inventories to Rs 443 crore. At record prices, customers stretch terms; if
copper corrects, receivables follow with a lag and impairments would follow them. Watch
days sales outstanding (FY25: 30d; FY26: 16d; Sep-26: ~22d at annualised volumes).
Dilution overhang and OFS pricing: the 6.00% government OFS cleared in August (floor
Rs 514, a 10.4% discount to the prior close of Rs 573.55; indicative clearing Rs 532.42;
retail book ~7.3x covered; 25,000-share employee offer), and the QIP (~10% more) will set
price and timing. Any QIP done below today’s price would be dilutive to our EPS ladder;
done above it, it changes the math we show.
Commodity-specific: ore grades decline and Malanjkhand’s deep underground expansion
(paste-fill plant, battery-electric LHDs) is technically demanding; water and power costs;
the CCEA-approved 12.2 MTPA plan assumes approvals and contractors performing to
Policy and environment: mining royalty and cess (Rs 276 crore, ~9% of FY26 revenue) can
be raised; the Gujarat Copper Project’s lease deed is pending execution with a writ in the
Gujarat High Court (gross carrying value Rs 48 crore); 21-Nov-2025 Labour Codes raise
Upside risks: copper above $14,000 into FY28 (our Bull: FY28E EPS Rs 21.22; Dec-27
value Rs 249); on-time 12.2 MTPA delivery with Government support; re-rating if the OFS
overhang clears and the QIP lands at/above the market price; index inclusion flows.

Our Dec-27 price target of Rs 145 rests on a three-stage discounted cash-flow model (FCFF at 25.17% unlevered tax; terminal growth 5.0%; terminal EBIT margin
30.0% of total income) at a 13.75% WACC, rolled forward from the 30-Sep-26 balance-sheet date and less Rs 3.36 per share of dividends expected to Dec-27 (Rs
1.86 FY26 final, paid Oct-Nov 26, plus an assumed Rs 1.50 FY27 interim; our FY27 total DPS assumption is Rs 3.00 vs Rs 2.86 in FY26; FY28/29 assumed Rs
3.50; no company guidance exists for these figures). The alternatives we computed and considered, printed in this report, are: (i) the 5-year monthly beta variant of
the cost of equity (15.6%): Rs 120; (ii) the switch to peer multiples (nearest domestic metal CPSEs, forward P/E 6.4x-10.1x, EV/EBITDA 3.5x-6.8x): broadly Rs
190-230 for Hindustan Copper at equal multiples, still below the price; (iii) the reverse DCF, which assigns no achievable value to the price within any terminal
margin or stage-2 growth shift at our WACC — see pages 4-6. None of these changes the rating; none is hidden. This report’s sole valuation output is the DCF-
